section_summary: This section documents the rising tide of nationalism, militarism, and ideological orthodoxy in Japan between late 1935 and February 1936, highlighted by analyses of the concept of 'Nippon Kokutai' and Embassy Tokyo's comprehensive evaluation of domestic and international forces facing the empire at the start of 1936. Diplomatic reporting covers internal political tensions, economic nationalism in petroleum and automotive industries, continental expansionist pressures in North China and Mongolia, and discussions with Foreign Office officials on the Army's destabilizing influence. The section culminates in urgent diplomatic telegrams and Department memoranda reporting the outbreak of the February 26, 1936 military coup d'état in Tokyo, including the assassination of prominent statesmen, the seizure of government buildings by rebel army officers, and immediate American and international reactions.

subfiles.about: Concluding pages of a diplomatic despatch evaluating Japanese legislation on automobile production, compulsory Shintoism in schools, petroleum industry controls, and growing diplomatic intransigence.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details War Office efforts to foster domestic automobile self-sufficiency for wartime readiness while obstructing foreign companies. He discusses the Education Ministry's push to officially recognize Shintoism as a state religion and mandate its doctrines and shrines in all Japanese schools, contrary to past policies separating religion from public education. The despatch also highlights Japan's uncompromising stance toward foreign oil firms under the Petroleum Industry Control Law and notes an increasingly intractable attitude in dealings with foreign powers.
subfiles.title: Despatch on Japanese Automotive and Petroleum Legislation, Shinto Education Policies, and Rising Nationalism

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording a War Department compilation of notes regarding Japan prepared for Secretary of War Dern's visit.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet references file 033.1190 Dern, George H./46, dated September 19, 1935, from the War Department. It records the preparation of a compilation of information and notes regarding Japan for the use of Secretary of War George H. Dern during his proposed visit to the Japanese Empire.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Notes on Japan for Secretary George H. Dern (033.1190 Dern, George H./46)

subfiles.about: A cover memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck urging Secretary of State Cordell Hull to read an attached analysis of Japanese militarism and national psychology.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, submits a two-page memorandum on Japanese thought and psychology to Secretary of State Cordell Hull. Hornbeck warns that few Americans adequately comprehend what the world faces with a militant Japan on the move. He expresses the desire that the American public be provided more information to foster greater understanding of the inevitable realities of Japanese policy.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Secretary of State Regarding Japanese Thought and Militant Psychology

subfiles.about: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing the nationalist and mystical doctrine of 'Nippon Kokutai' (Japanism) and its aggressive international implications.
subfiles.summary: W. T. Turner analyzes two pamphlets on 'Nippon Kokutai' published by Chigaku Tanaka, president of the reactionary Meijikai society. He excerpts passages asserting that Japan possesses unique moral principles destined to serve as a model for world peace and that Nippon has an unavoidable mission to oversee the world. Turner compares these mystical doctrines to writings by General Sadao Araki, warning that such cultish beliefs in divine descent and imperial infallibility foster a dangerous crusading urge born of an inferiority complex and historic insularity.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding 'Nippon Kokutai' or Japanism

subfiles.about: An ideological English-language pamphlet by Chigaku Tanaka explaining the divine foundation, unique characteristics, and global mission of Japan's national polity (Kokutai).
subfiles.summary: Chigaku Tanaka outlines the external form and substance of 'Nippon Kokutai,' tracing the origins of the state to the Sun Goddess, divine creation, and Emperor Jimmu. He posits five fundamental elements of the empire—Gods, Michi (the Way), Emperors, Subjects, and Land—and asserts that countries lacking Kokutai are unfinished entities sustained merely by physical force or money. He details the three principles of Accumulation of Happiness, Amassment of Glories, and Cultivation of Righteousness, arguing that Japan is destined to serve as the supreme exemplar of justice and peace for the entire world.
subfiles.title: What is Nippon Kokutai? Introduction to Nipponese National Principles (No. 2)

subfiles.about: A comprehensive diplomatic survey and evaluation of economic, financial, domestic political, and foreign policy forces shaping Japan at the start of 1936.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a detailed assessment of Japan's economic prosperity in 1935, driven by corporate earnings, export growth, and agricultural recovery, balanced against growing government debt and economic nationalism. In domestic affairs, he reviews controversy surrounding the 'Emperor organ' theory and the upcoming general election. In foreign affairs, he examines Japanese expansionism in North China and Inner Mongolia, tension with Outer Mongolia and the Soviet Union, and the moderating role of the Emperor and senior statesmen. He concludes that Japan's underlying expansionist drive in East Asia will persist, influenced by demographic pressure and the quest for raw materials, though cultural milestones like the planned 1940 Tokyo Olympics offer potential avenues for international engagement.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1630: General Situation Facing Japan at the Opening of the Year 1936

subfiles.about: A diplomatic instruction from the Department of State commending Ambassador Grew and Embassy Tokyo for their comprehensive annual appraisal of Japan's situation.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State cordially commends Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and his embassy staff for confidential Despatch No. 1630 of January 7, 1936. The Secretary assures the embassy that appraisals executed with such thoroughness and thought are of great practical value to the Department.
subfiles.title: Instruction Commending Despatch No. 1630 on the General Situation Facing Japan

subfiles.about: An analytical table of contents indexing the topics and page numbers of Confidential Despatch No. 1630.
subfiles.summary: This document provides a topical index for Despatch No. 1630, listing subject sections and page references. It outlines economic and financial conditions, domestic and foreign political developments across North China, Mongolia, and the Siberian border, and an evaluation of forces including the Emperor, military, business, population growth, and expansionist trends.
subfiles.title: Index to Despatch No. 1630

subfiles.about: An internal Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo's Despatch No. 1645 concerning conversations with Saburo Kurusu on the Japanese military.
subfiles.summary: This Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 1645 regarding conversations between Erle R. Dickover and Saburo Kurusu of the Japanese Foreign Office. It notes Kurusu's view that Japanese military officers are well-intentioned and sought to end political corruption, but are unsuited to direct economic and social systems. The memorandum reports Kurusu's impression that Army leaders are slowly recognizing their limitations and that the administration of Manchuria served as a sobering lesson.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Summarizing Despatch No. 1645 on the Position and Influence of the Military in Japanese Politics

subfiles.about: A diplomatic despatch from Ambassador Grew transmitting an embassy memorandum of conversations with Saburo Kurusu concerning the military's role in government.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits a memorandum prepared by Erle R. Dickover detailing conversations with Saburo Kurusu, Chief of the Foreign Office Commercial Affairs Bureau. Grew notes Kurusu's conviction that the Army should not attempt to govern or reorganize the state, as doing so would breed corruption within military ranks and destroy public trust. Grew observes that while informed Japanese agree with Kurusu, the military and reactionary factions do not share this viewpoint.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1645: Transmitting Memorandum of Conversation on the Military in Japanese Politics

subfiles.about: An embassy memorandum recording conversations with Saburo Kurusu regarding the mentality, limitations, and political influence of the Japanese military.
subfiles.summary: Erle R. Dickover records discussions with Saburo Kurusu, who characterizes Army officers as sincere but simplistic and devoid of constructive political or economic programs. Kurusu describes using parables to warn military figures that the Army should sweep out political corruption but leave the arrangement of state governance to experts. He recounts conversations with Generals Tetsuzan Nagata and Takashi Hishikari, notes that difficulties in attracting capital to Manchuria have exposed the military's lack of omniscience, and expresses doubt that party government can soon return.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversations with Saburo Kurusu on the Position and Influence of the Military in Japanese Politics

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 1649 concerning the dissolution of the Imperial Diet and the prospects for Japan's nationalistic foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet references Despatch No. 1649, dated January 22, 1936, from Ambassador Grew. It concerns the dissolution of the Diet and Japan's internal political situation, concluding there is no reason to anticipate any material change in nationalistic foreign policy even if the Seiyukai party wins the general election and overthrows the Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Despatch No. 1649 on the Dissolution of the Diet (894.032/149)

subfiles.about: An urgent initial telegram from Ambassador Grew reporting that Japanese military forces seized partial control of Tokyo and assassinated several prominent officials.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew sends an urgent test code telegram reporting that the military took partial possession of the Japanese Government and the city of Tokyo early in the morning of February 26. He notes that several prominent men were reportedly assassinated, though confirmation remains impossible due to a total blackout on foreign news dispatches and telephone calls.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 36 Reporting Military Seizure of Government Buildings and Assassinations in Tokyo

subfiles.about: A State Department telegram acknowledging receipt of Ambassador Grew's initial reports on the military coup in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State confirms receipt of Ambassador Grew's telegram No. 36 sent at 10 a.m. on February 26, as well as the first three sections of his telegram No. 37 sent at noon.
subfiles.title: Telegram Acknowledging Receipt of Tokyo Telegrams Nos. 36 and 37

subfiles.about: A diplomatic instruction directing Ambassador Grew to convey official American condolences to the Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs following the assassinations.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull instructs Ambassador Grew to deliver a personal message to the Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs. The message expresses deep regret on behalf of the American Government and people upon learning of the deaths of distinguished Japanese officials and extends sincere condolences.
subfiles.title: Telegram Transmitting Condolences on the Deaths of Japanese Officials

subfiles.about: A comprehensive four-section telegram detailing the assassination of senior Japanese officials, rebel troop movements, public manifestos, and political aims of the February 26 coup.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports the confirmed assassinations of former Premier Admiral Saito and General Watanabe, alongside attacks on Count Makino, Admiral Suzuki, and Finance Minister Takahashi. He describes military cordons surrounding Tokyo government offices, the suspension of communications, and the distribution of an insurgent manifesto signed by Captains Nonaka and Ando denouncing treaty compromises and demanding a 'Showa restoration.' Grew characterizes the uprising as a young officer fascist coup intended to eliminate moderate elder statesmen surrounding the Emperor, identifies General Mazaki as a reported leading spirit, and notes that Admiral Osumi assumed the role of acting Prime Minister.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 37 (Sections 1-4) on the Military Coup d'État, Assassinations, and Rebel Manifesto

subfiles.about: A confidential paraphrase of Section 4 of Ambassador Grew's Telegram No. 37 analyzing the origins and leadership of the Tokyo coup.
subfiles.summary: This Department paraphrase summarizes Grew's report that the coup d'état was launched by young fascist army officers aiming to eliminate imperial advisers and achieve the 'Showa restoration.' It notes that the Emperor was held incommunicado to prevent countermanding decrees, attributes the revolt to nationalist agitation following recent liberal election victories and the Aizawa court-martial, and reports that Count Makino survived while Admiral Osumi assumed acting premiership.
subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Section 4 of Telegram No. 37

subfiles.about: A diplomatic telegram from Ambassador Bullitt in Moscow reporting Soviet Foreign Commissar Litvinov's and Chinese Ambassador Yen's assessments of the Japanese general elections.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Bullitt reports that Soviet Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov expressed surprise and satisfaction over the Minseito Party's victory in the Japanese elections, believing it reflected popular opposition to military adventures and would improve Soviet-Japanese relations. Chinese Ambassador W. W. Yen observed that while the election results would not alter Japan's fundamental aggressive stance toward China, they might result in a more suave diplomatic procedure.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 64 from Moscow on Soviet and Chinese Reactions to Japanese Election Results

subfiles.about: A confidential paraphrase of Ambassador Bullitt's telegram summarizing Soviet and Chinese diplomatic reactions to the Japanese elections.
subfiles.summary: This Department paraphrase re-states the contents of Moscow Telegram No. 64. It records Litvinov's optimism that the Minseito victory demonstrated public resistance to military adventurism, thereby reducing border friction, and relays Ambassador Yen's assessment that Japanese policy toward China would become smoother in execution without altering underlying objectives.
subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 64 from Moscow

subfiles.about: A two-section telegram detailing the strength of rebel troops in Tokyo, government emergency meetings at the Imperial Palace, and insurgent political demands.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew relays reliable confidential information that approximately 1,000 junior officers and soldiers from the First Division seized the Prime Minister's residence, police headquarters, War Department, and General Staff offices, while raiding residences to murder senior statesmen. He reports that Prince Saionji and Count Makino escaped, while uninjured Cabinet and War Council members convened with the Emperor at the Imperial Palace. Insurgents refused to surrender government buildings, demanding the appointment of Admiral Kanji Kato or Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma as Premier, while loyal troop reinforcements were summoned into Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 38 (Sections 1-2) on Insurgent Troop Positions, Government Consultations, and Political Demands

subfiles.about: A transmittal letter from Secretary of State Cordell Hull providing President Franklin D. Roosevelt with Embassy Tokyo's initial reports on the military coup.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull transmits copies of Ambassador Grew's Telegrams Nos. 36, 37, and 38 regarding the Tokyo military coup to President Roosevelt. Hull includes an interpretive memorandum prepared by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs and notes that the State Department is refraining from public comment beyond expressing regret over the assassinations.
subfiles.title: Letter from the Secretary of State to President Roosevelt Transmitting Tokyo Coup Telegrams
